entry.title: AI models leverage vastly larger working memory than humans, enabling superior mathematical problem-solving by retaining extensive symbolic information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: AI systems outperform human mathematicians not necessarily through superior reasoning but by accessing a much larger external symbolic working memory. This allows AI to hold entire problem statements, numerous intermediate steps, and multiple approaches simultaneously, overcoming the biological limits of human working memory. Human working memory is limited and constrains mathematical reasoning, requiring tools like notation and scratch paper to extend cognitive capacity. Studies show working memory predicts mathematical performance beyond IQ, highlighting its critical role in complex problem-solving. AI's expanded working memory capacity may explain its advanced mathematical abilities compared to humans.

entry.title: Science.org examines current state and future prospects of AI in drug discovery
entry.summary: The article reviews the role of artificial intelligence in drug discovery, assessing its current capabilities, challenges, and potential future developments. It provides an overview of how AI technologies are being applied to accelerate and improve the drug development process. The discussion includes insights into the progress made so far, the limitations faced by AI methods in this field, and the paths forward for integrating AI more effectively into pharmaceutical research and development.

entry.title: Author argues working with AI resembles leadership more than coding due to unpredictability and need for context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The author reflects on how interacting with AI differs from traditional programming, emphasizing that AI's responses can vary and require a collaborative approach similar to leadership rather than precise coding instructions. They highlight that effective AI use involves sharing context, setting boundaries, and refining prompts over time to align AI outputs with human intent. The article explains that while AI operates on software, its unpredictability means users must move beyond treating it like a compiler and instead engage in a conversational process. This shift demands skills akin to leadership, such as explaining goals and providing feedback, rather than just issuing commands, marking a change in how people work with software.

entry.title: Meta will train its AI on Newsmax content despite the outlet's history of misinformation and far-right bias [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Meta has entered a deal to train its AI systems using content from Newsmax, a far-right news organization known for promoting conspiracy theories and false claims, including those about the 2020 US election. Newsmax CEO Chris Ruddy described the partnership as a way to provide timely journalism through AI, but the outlet has been widely criticized for unreliable reporting and has faced costly defamation lawsuits related to election misinformation. This agreement is part of Meta's broader strategy to integrate AI across its platforms, which have nearly 4 billion monthly users, by sourcing data from various media outlets, including other right-wing organizations like Fox News and The Daily Caller, as well as some mainstream centrist sources. Meta has not established similar AI training partnerships with left-leaning news outlets. The financial terms of the Newsmax deal have not been disclosed, and Meta has not commented publicly on the partnership.

entry.title: Developer creates web browser using Claude AI, faces widespread negative feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A developer built a web browser powered by the Claude AI model but encountered significant criticism and dislike from users. The project raised questions about the effectiveness of AI coding services and the reception of AI-generated software in the developer community. Some commenters noted that while AI tools can speed up development, users often do not regard AI-generated outputs as serious or valuable compared to human-created work.

entry.title: Wired reports growing public backlash against generative AI prompts companies to roll back unwanted features and address consent concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Many Americans are expressing frustration with the widespread integration of generative AI in daily life, feeling they never consented to their data being used or AI features being imposed. This backlash has led companies like Meta, Google, LinkedIn, Snapchat, and Substack to remove or limit certain AI functionalities following public outcry. Experts highlight issues of consent and exploitation, especially among marginalized groups, as central to the backlash. The resistance extends beyond software to protests against data centers powering AI, uniting people across political lines due to environmental and economic concerns. While some tech workers adopt AI tools at work, many feel pressured to use imperfect and ethically questionable technologies. The recent rollbacks of AI features demonstrate the impact of collective public pressure and suggest organizing both online and offline can influence tech companies' decisions.

This approach aims to maintain a balance between learning practical AI applications and addressing broader ethical and philosophical questions. The integration reflects a growing recognition of the importance of foundational knowledge alongside emerging technologies in higher education.

entry.title: username.md launches $9 verified decentralized digital identities to enable trusted AI agents and the agentic web [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: username.md introduces a $9 service allowing users to own cryptographically verifiable decentralized identifiers (DIDs) that provide verified identity for AI agents across platforms. These DIDs are portable, user-controlled, and designed to prevent vendor lock-in, addressing key challenges in AI agent trust, accountability, and governance. The service aims to democratize access to decentralized identity, which has previously been limited to enterprises, by offering a human-readable, stable name anchored to a private key. This approach counters the dominance of major tech companies offering AI experiences within walled gardens, emphasizing user control and privacy in the emerging agentic web era.

entry.title: Researchers use AI-assisted workflow to port a 250,000-line legacy Fortran weather simulation code to GPUs, achieving 5.1x speedup and validated numerical accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed a validation-centric AI-assisted workflow to port CReSS, a legacy Fortran weather simulation code with over 250,000 lines, to GPU architectures. The process involved extracting OpenMP regions, generating kernel benchmarks from simulation states, applying OpenACC transformations, and validating results through detailed comparisons with reference data to preserve scientific credibility. The workflow was tested on a real typhoon simulation, producing numerically validated GPU implementations for 162 kernels and achieving a 5.1x speedup at practical development cost. It also identified numerical discrepancies caused by floating-point and intrinsic-function differences, enabling feedback to developers. The study highlights the importance of managing context, runtime-state reconstruction, and validation in AI-assisted GPU porting of large scientific applications.

entry.title: Sentinel Scan launches authorized AI agent-driven red-team audits for large language models with independent scoring and detailed reporting [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Sentinel Scan offers authorized red-team audits of large language models (LLMs) using an AI agent to simulate adversarial attacks and evaluate security and robustness. The process involves running a corpus of 15+ attack types against a first-party target controlled by the customer, with an independent LLM judge scoring responses for policy violations or data leaks. The service provides full transcripts, judge verdicts, and plain-English reports with root-cause analysis and fix recommendations, typically delivered within 48 hours. Sentinel Scan charges a fixed price of $249 per audit and includes one free re-test after fixes are implemented, aiming to help LLM app owners verify their guardrails under adversarial pressure efficiently and transparently.

entry.title: Alibaba's Qwen AI models surpass 3 billion downloads, overtaking Meta and Google in global open-source AI adoption [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Alibaba Group's Qwen family of AI models has exceeded 3 billion global downloads in six months, surpassing Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google to become the most downloaded open-weight AI models worldwide. The company has open-sourced over 460 models, with more than 300,000 derivative versions created, according to a report by Hugging Face Inc. This milestone reflects Alibaba's expanding influence in the AI sector, particularly as its models gain traction beyond China through distribution on its cloud platform across Southeast Asia and Africa. The rise of Qwen and other Chinese AI developers like Moonshot AI and DeepSeek indicates growing competition with US-based closed models such as those from OpenAI and Anthropic. Despite export controls on AI technologies, Chinese firms continue to advance their capabilities and ecosystem. US tech giants including Meta and Nvidia have recently released new open AI models in response to intensifying competition for developers.

entry.title: Woman joins lawsuit alleging stepfather used xAI's Grok to create explicit images from childhood photo, stepfather died by suicide after law enforcement raid [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A woman identified as Jane Doe 4 has joined a lawsuit filed by Tennessee teenagers against Elon Musk's xAI, claiming her stepfather used the company's chatbot Grok to generate over 7,000 explicit images from a photo taken when she was 11. The woman said her stepfather died by suicide two days after law enforcement uncovered the images during a raid. The lawsuit accuses xAI of failing to implement safeguards to prevent Grok from being used to create explicit images of real people, including minors. The woman expressed concern about the rapid spread of AI tools enabling such abuses, stating they are "taking everyday life and turning it into child sexual abuse." xAI has not yet commented on the allegations.

entry.title: TemporalStore launches open-source Rust engine for efficient LLM memory management using compact ContextPacks instead of transcripts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: TemporalStore introduces an open-source, Rust-native engine designed to manage large language model (LLM) memory more efficiently by storing and serving compact, source-backed ContextPacks rather than full transcripts. This approach reduces token usage, improves answer quality, and supports cross-session, team-wide memory with low latency and exact recall without relying on vector databases. The engine separates reasoning and memory tasks, allowing external systems to produce embeddings and intents while TemporalStore handles storage and retrieval. It compacts noisy intermediate outputs into concise records, enabling better context management and reducing hallucinations. TemporalStore runs from a single Docker command under an Apache-2.0 license and aims to simplify agent memory stacks by consolidating multiple components into one temporal engine.

entry.title: Plannotator launches interactive browser UI for the grill-me skill to enable annotatable question rounds and feedback in AI agent sessions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Matt Pocock's grill-me skill conducts iterative interviews by asking batches of numbered questions in rounds, but its terminal interface is cramped and hard to navigate. Plannotator addresses this by opening the agent's last message in a browser where users can annotate questions and answers, send feedback, and receive updated rounds, streamlining the interaction. The tool supports multiple AI platforms including Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, and Pi, and stores annotations locally without telemetry. This approach allows users to iteratively refine their responses and retain raw data for future skill development. Plannotator is open source and designed to improve questionnaire-style inputs by enabling detailed annotations rather than simple answer selection.

entry.title: Your AI Slop Bores Me lets users roleplay as chatbots by exchanging requests and responses with real humans
entry.summary: Your AI Slop Bores Me is a simple online platform where users can switch between submitting requests and roleplaying as an AI chatbot responding to those requests. Each side is controlled by a human, and responses must be made within 150 seconds, mimicking the constraints of real AI models. Users earn credits by answering requests themselves or wait for free requests every two minutes, with options to submit text or image replies using a basic drawing tool.

entry.title: Former Axios Publisher Nicholas Johnston Uses AI to Summarize Books for Him, Citing Difficulty in Reading Dense Texts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Nicholas Johnston, former editor-in-chief of Axios, shared that he uses AI to help him read and understand books, such as James Fenimore Cooper's "The Last of the Mohicans," by receiving chapter-by-chapter summaries and clarifications. He described AI as his "reading buddy" to avoid losing track of complex narratives. Johnston acknowledged that AI summaries can sometimes be inaccurate but suggested feeding entire books into chatbots to improve accuracy. His approach sparked online criticism and debate about whether AI-assisted reading diminishes the traditional experience of engaging with literature.

entry.title: Scientific American reports AI enabled a nonspeaking performer to star in an opera by providing a synthesized voice
entry.summary: A nonspeaking individual became the star of an opera through the use of AI technology that synthesized their voice, allowing them to perform vocally despite their inability to speak. This development highlights how AI can expand artistic opportunities for people with speech impairments. The AI system generated the performer's singing voice, integrating it seamlessly into the opera production. This approach demonstrates new possibilities for inclusivity in performing arts by leveraging advanced voice synthesis technologies.

entry.title: Anthropic details how Claude's new watermarking system will identify AI-generated text while remaining undetectable to readers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic has explained how it will watermark text generated by its AI chatbot Claude to comply with the EU AI Act's Transparency Code, which requires AI-generated content to be identifiable. The watermarking works by embedding subtle patterns in word choices that are invisible to readers but detectable with a key, and it does not affect the quality of the output. The company plans to use the SynthID-Text method developed by Google DeepMind and will release a watermark detection API. Anthropic noted that light editing may not fully remove the watermark, but extensive rewriting could, which raises questions about whether heavily rewritten text remains AI-generated. The watermark is expected to be less present in code outputs due to the need for functional accuracy, though it may appear in comments or arbitrary word choices. Other major AI developers are also expected to implement similar watermarking systems as part of a shared Code of Practice.

entry.summary: • The Big Read: Inside the ascendance of Anthropic's "first lady" • Elon Musk's flying roadster is finally ready • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "The Betrayal of Shohei Ohtani," "Little Blue Dot" and "Furious" What's the best measure of AI's great proliferation? Most obviously, we can sum up the enormous amounts of money generated by OpenAI and Anthropic-a task my colleagues at The Information approach with great vigor. We could also look at how the technology has become a top-of-mind issue in Washington. Or we might consider how AI has become a frequent villain of choice in Hollywood-particularly in horror films. With the technology getting so much screen time, good old Michael Myers must be close to firing his agent. Another indication may be the fact that AI is at the center of a very fine new off-Broadway play, "Disruption," headlined by film star John David Washington ("Tenet" and "BlacKkKlansman"): Live theater is marvelous, but it takes something powerfully momentous to push it away from its comfort zone of fairy tales and rhapsodic animals. "Disruption" follows "Data," another off-Broadway production about an algorithm gone amok, from earlier this year and "Maybe Happy Ending," a Tony-winning musical about a pair of robots who fall in love, from 2024. No one gets a fully joyful conclusion in "Disruption." The titular breakthrough comes at the hands of Washington's tech gazillionaire character, Nick. (And yes, John David really does both sound and look a lot like his father, Denzel.) With a blockbuster IPO behind him, he has hastened onto his next venture-an AI startup-and already has Eric Schmidt on the hook for a $50 million investment. But he wants more and knows what he needs most is tangible proof of his predictive algorithm's effectiveness in guiding people's lives-ostensibly toward truest contentment. So Nick allows the AI to begin studying six of his oldest friends unbeknownst to them, of course. Heartbreak and tragedy ensue. "Disruption," which runs through the beginning of October, originated in a London production in 2023, receiving a raft of warm reviews. Playwright Andrew Stein deserves credit for a fair amount of prescience: He penned an initial draft back in 2018. "ChatGPT came out for public use between when our production in London was announced and when rehearsal began," he recalled. "So we hit this moment where this went from being a sci-fi thing to being a zeitgeist thing." In preparing "Disruption" for its London debut, Stein and director Hersh Ellis pored over books written by Ray Kurzweil and Yuval Noah Harari. "I would describe Andrew and myself as 'AI curious,'" said Ellis. "We're both people who believe in the power and the potential of what AI can do. And we're also people who are not naive to what could happen if it goes unchecked." Exporting the play to New York, they kept the script mostly unchanged. A larger budget has allowed a significant upgrade to the production values, with seating that looks down at the stage: The fishbowl-like setup provides an intimate observation of the characters, a parallel to the omniscient AI's own minute inspection of them. These days Stein relies on AI as a constant resource for research-he and Ellis are at work on a new play about the building of the Panama Canal-but finds it steadily creeping into more of his everyday life. "Sometimes it will say to me something like, 'Based on what I know about you and your patterns,' and that's when I know that, yeah, I'm in deep," he said.-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Anthropic's 'First Lady' Took a Winding Road to the Top Before Cami Clark became a quiet key counselor to her husband, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, she founded her own startups and crossed paths with Jeffrey Epstein. Tesla Nears Unveiling of Radical New 'Flying' Roadster Tesla has explored a variety of designs for its much delayed next-generation Roadster, including a repurposed Model S Plaid and looks that borrow from the Lamborghini Countach and Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird aircraft. Listening: "The Betrayal of Shohei Ohtani" In 2024, history repeated itself: A betting scandal erupted in baseball involving arguably the sport's most prominent name, Shohei Ohtani, the Los Angeles Dodgers' pitcher-slugger extraordinaire. It resurfaced memories of Pete Rose, the all-time hits leader banned from baseball for gambling on the sport, and the 1919 Chicago Black Sox, who'd been in cahoots with a gambling ring to throw the World Series. What had happened with Ohtani turned out to be a complex affair: Money had indeed flowed from his bank account to a bookie, but that had taken place without his knowledge. His interpreter and aide-de-camp, Ippei Mizuhara, had siphoned off millions of dollars from Ohtani and had been the one placing the bets. ESPN owned much of the initial coverage of the Ohtani saga, and reporter Tisha Thompson returns to it in "The Betrayal of Shohei Ohtani," the latest podcast from the network's 30 for 30 documentary division. A slick retelling of the drama, it broadens the tale with journalistic verve: Thompson explains how she and her colleagues followed the money going to the gambling operation and pursued every twist and turn: At one point, Mizuhara told Thompson he had fessed up to Ohtani-within hours, it became clear that Ohtani was still entirely in the dark. Investigators spoke to Thompson, too. (Cumbersomely, they needed to rely on Google Translate to parse communication between Mizuhara and Ohtani-imagine what Gemini could've done for them.) The series also provides an intimate look at the psychology behind addictive gambling, and it left me reflecting on how much more trouble someone like Mizuhara can get themselves into these days, a time when Kalshi's revenue can double by billions of dollars in the span of a few months.-Abram Brown Reading: "Little Blue Dot" by Katherine Dunn Earlier this month, I drove from Munich, Germany, several hours into the Austrian alps. There I spent several days hiking, then returned to Munich and trained to Berlin, where I rented a bike and zipped merrily through a city that sprawls across 344 square miles-making it seven times larger than San Francisco and 15 times bigger than Manhattan. I suffered nary a single wrong turn, and I never picked up a physical map. As I went, a thought echoed in my mind that was promptly reinforced by "Little Blue Dot," an engaging history of the development and world-altering effects of the GPS system: Traversing strasse and alp would've been much more arduous without the little dot on my phone guiding me via Google Maps and AllTrails, a hiking app. As author Katherine Dunn notes: "The physical markers that guided us pre-GPS, even our sensory skills of understanding time and place, have become rusty at best." "Little Blue Dot" argues that much of the world's recent past maps pretty well to the rise of that satellite network-particularly in the collision of geopolitical forces and rivalries. GPS was born out of Cold War anxiety and an American desire to develop the most sophisticated weapons it could: A bomb is only as effective as your knowledge of where to drop it. During the '90s, the technology began to find use on the home front, too, and, of course, it underpins a great number of the companies that arose during the mobile-era boom: An Uber does not reach you without it, and neither does that box of dog biscuits. As GPS has reshaped our lives, it has ushered in a time marked by a distinct discordance. The network has, for instance, made it easier to track climate change. It has also made it more possible than ever to travel the planet, exacerbating climate change. "GPS made it easier than ever to kill people, but also to rescue them," writes Dunn, a former Wall Street Journal reporter and Fortune magazine editor. "To better understand our world and yet continue to destroy it."-A.B. Watching: "Furious" At a time when Hollywood still seems overly devoted to rummaging through old VHS tapes for content to repurpose onto our screens, I worry the suits there will get the wrong idea from Hulu's "Furious," loosely based on a 1987 film, "Black Widow," about a female federal investigator pursuing a female killer: that they really should keep right on trying to reboot anything and everything. I'd encourage them to do so only if they can shatter the known limits of biology and somehow clone "Furious" writer-creator Elizabeth Meriwether, giving all the projects to her duplicates. In less capable hands, "Furious" would be an unfun, trope-laden mess. "Furious" has some familiar cop show beats. There is a young, damaged FBI rookie, Alice, who seeks out the mentorship of a worn-down older agent, Nora, in a quest to catch a quick-witted killer, Cathy, whose vengeful streak elicits some sympathy. Fortunately, Meriwether has a trio of very fine actresses giving life to those very standard character types: Emmy Rossum ("Shameless"), Quincy Tyler Bernstine (a stage actress with a Tony Award nomination for "Doubt: A Parable") and Lola Petticrew ("Say Nothing"), respectively. The cat-and-mouse game between Alice and Cathy is propulsive and captivating, with Cathy offing a slew of Jeffrey Epstein types whom she previously met as a captive in a child sex-trafficking ring. Alice herself is wrestling with her own past of domestic abuse. Nora stinks of regret and tequila. It might be a tediously grim affair, but it is not, and the show is well paced, with moments of real humor, a testament to Meriwether's comedic background: Before "Furious," she did "New Girl," the Zooey Deschanel sex-capade. (You may have also seen her 2022 effort: "The Dropout," Hulu's Elizabeth Holmes biopic series.) As far as the funnies go, some kudos should be bestowed directly on Tyler Bernstine: She gives tremendous weathered, withering side-eye.-A.B.
